text: This lesson builds the actual two-qubit variational classifier for the Iris subproblem chosen last lesson, using two real Iris measurements, and traces one full forward pass and one gradient update by hand — the capstone project's core technical step.

The circuit uses two qubits, one for petal length, one for petal width, angle-encoded, followed by a trainable RY rotation on each qubit and a CNOT entangling them, then measures the expectation value of Z on qubit one for the prediction. Using real measurements scaled to radians by a fixed factor of 0.3: a Setosa sample at 1.4 and 0.2 centimeters becomes angles 0.42 and 0.06, and a Versicolor sample at 4.7 and 1.4 centimeters becomes 1.41 and 0.42.

Running the full circuit with an untrained ansatz, both rotation angles set to 0.5: the Setosa sample gives an expectation value of 0.6058, a probability of 0.8029 — confidently wrong, since its true label is zero, producing a loss of about 1.6241. The Versicolor sample gives a probability of 0.3336, also leaning wrong, with a loss of about 1.0977. Both losses are large, which is expected for an arbitrary, untrained starting point.

Computing one parameter-shift gradient step using the Setosa sample: the gradient of the circuit output with respect to the first rotation angle comes out to about negative 0.7956, chaining through to a loss gradient of about negative 2.0184. Updating with a learning rate of 0.4 moves that angle to about 1.3073. Re-running the forward pass for Setosa with this updated angle drops the loss from about 1.6241 down to about 0.5483 — a large, genuine, verified improvement from one gradient step on real data.
Next lesson is the one that makes the whole project honest: actually measuring this quantum classifier against a classical baseline on held-out real data, and reporting exactly what happens.
